fmt_hopr.x: El formato de entrada de HORSES3D y FLEXI, el que escribe PyHOPE. Es el más cómodo: los hexaedros ya vienen en orden tensorial, que es el canónico de LEGOLAS, y cada elemento trae sus seis caras en orden CGNS con el vecino y la BC.

Dos detalles que el lector resuelve por ti. `NodeCoords` repite cada nodo una vez por elemento que lo usa; los únicos salen de `GlobalNodeIDs`. Y una zona interior (BCType 100, como `rotor_cylinder`) lleva la BC escrita en **las dos** caras que se tocan: LEGOLAS la guarda una sola vez.
`meta['file_cell_index']` da, para cada celda de LEGOLAS, el elemento del fichero (desde 0). Súmale uno y tienes el número que imprime HORSES3D, por ejemplo el «peor elemento» de una prueba FSP.

fmt_cgns.x: Un `.cgns` moderno es un fichero HDF5 con un árbol de nodos CGNS dentro, así que se lee con h5py y no hace falta instalar la librería CGNS. Se leen las zonas no estructuradas, las secciones de cualquier tipo o `MIXED` y las BC de `ZoneBC` (por caras o por vértices). Si no hay `ZoneBC`, cada sección de superficie se convierte en una BC con su nombre.
Los hexaedros tensoriales (HEXA_8/27/64/125) se reordenan al orden canónico. Los serendípitos (HEXA_20…) solo conservan las esquinas, y lo avisan.
Lo que no se lee: CGNS/ADF (el formato antiguo, que no es HDF5: se convierte con `adf2hdf`), zonas estructuradas y poliedros NGON/NFACE.

fmt_gmsh.x: La versión 2.2 se lee con un parser propio porque **ANSA escribe el binario en big-endian**. El formato lo permite: el entero `1` de la cabecera indica el orden de bytes, y gmsh lo respeta. meshio no, y falla con un escueto «Couldn't read file». `meta['byteorder']` te dice cuál era. La versión 4 sigue pasando por meshio.

Los grupos físicos dan los nombres: los de dimensión 3 son zonas y los de dimensión 2 son BC. Un grupo físico declarado sin elementos aparece igualmente, como BC vacía. Las superficies que no están en ningún grupo físico se agrupan por entidad geométrica (`entity_<n>`).

fmt_hmesh.x: Los nodos de **solución** que usó HORSES3D, elemento a elemento. No hay conectividad ni BC: LEGOLAS la reconstruye fusionando los nodos que coinciden. Eso solo funciona con nodos de Gauss-Lobatto, que caen sobre las caras; con nodos de Gauss los elementos no comparten nada y lo avisa.
Ojo: aquí el orden es el de la solución (`p`), no el geométrico de la malla.

mesh.x: Contenedores

`Mesh` guarda `points` (los nodos únicos), `blocks` (una `CellBlock` por tipo y orden de elemento), `boundaries` (una `Boundary` por nombre), `zones` y `meta`. El índice global de una celda recorre los bloques en orden; para pasarlo a (bloque, local) está `mesh.locate_cell`.

Una `Boundary` **no tiene celdas de superficie**: guarda pares (elemento, cara local). Los nodos de la cara salen siempre del elemento de volumen, así que todos los formatos acaban con la misma disposición de caras, aunque el fichero escribiera las superficies a su manera.

nested_Quality.x: Dónde se evalúa

En los hexaedros de orden N, el jacobiano se calcula en los (N+1)³ puntos de Gauss-Lobatto a partir del interpolante de Lagrange por los nodos geométricos, que todos los formatos colocan **equiespaciados**; con N = 1 esos puntos son las esquinas. El volumen es la cuadratura de det J en esos puntos. En tetraedros, prismas y pirámides lineales se usan las tres aristas de cada esquina, normalizadas para que la celda regular valga 1 (el vértice de la pirámide tiene cuatro y se salta).

Orientación: VTK y gmsh numeran el prisma al revés, así que en un formato todos los prismas pueden salir «zurdos». Cada bloque se queda con la orientación de su mayoría y solo la minoría sale negativa; si un bloque se ha girado entero, lo dice un aviso `info`. Con las mallas de TIFON (prismas de CODA, gmsh 2.2) pasa siempre, y no es un error.
Comprobado con lo que ya sabíamos

Turbina g1, g2 y g4: `jacobian_ratio` mínimo 0,46, sin celdas negativas. Es lo mismo que dio PyHOPE con esas mallas (0,4–0,5). Las peores están en las esquinas de la malla en O alrededor del rotor (x = 3,66).

qué es

nested_Resolution.x: Con U = 1 y ν = L/Re, una longitud y vale y·Re·√(Cf/2)/L en unidades de pared. Cf sale de una correlación de placa plana: turbulenta 0,026·Re_x^(−1/7) o laminar (Blasius) 0,664·Re_x^(−1/2). Re_x usa la distancia de cada cara al borde de ataque (la esquina más aguas arriba de la zona) si se da `flow_dir`, y L si no. Es una estimación para dimensionar la primera celda, no una predicción del flujo: en un punto de remanso o en una zona desprendida falla por construcción.

El informe compara con los objetivos habituales de una LES que resuelve la pared (Piomelli & Chasnov 1996; Georgiadis, Rizzetta & Fureby 2010): y⁺ ≤ 1, Δx⁺ entre 50 y 150, Δz⁺ entre 15 y 40, y da el porcentaje de caras dentro de cada rango.

Cómo se lleva la solución a la malla

Un `.hsol` guarda, por elemento, la solución en (p+1)³ nodos de Gauss o de Gauss-Lobatto, en el orden de elementos del `.h5` de la malla. LEGOLAS evalúa el polinomio de cada elemento en los nodos geométricos de la malla (equiespaciados, orden Ngeo), y cada vértice que dibuja el visor toma el valor de **su** elemento: los saltos de una solución DG entre elementos se ven tal cual, sin promediar. Las variables primitivas (ρ, u, v, w, p, T, Mach, Cp y |V|) se calculan en los nodos de solución y después se interpolan.

Comprobado contra el propio solver (24/11/2026): la geometría de LEGOLAS evaluada en los nodos de solución reproduce las coordenadas del `.hmesh` de HORSES3D con un error de 10⁻¹⁴ (turbina, nodos de Gauss, p = 2, 3 y 4; esfera, Gauss-Lobatto, p = 2). El orden de elementos, el de nodos y su posición son los del solver.

how it is read
reading (20/11/2026)

turbine g4 (38,718 order-4 hexahedra, 2.5 M nodes): 0.6 s

fmt_hopr.x: The input format of HORSES3D and FLEXI, written by PyHOPE. The easiest one: hexahedra already come in tensor order, LEGOLAS's canonical one, and every element brings its six faces in CGNS order with neighbour and BC.

Two details the reader handles for you. `NodeCoords` repeats every node once per element using it; the unique ones come from `GlobalNodeIDs`. And an inner zone (BCType 100, like `rotor_cylinder`) has its BC written on **both** touching faces: LEGOLAS keeps it once.
`meta['file_cell_index']` gives, for every LEGOLAS cell, the element of the file (from 0). Add one and you get the number HORSES3D prints, e.g. the "worst element" of an FSP test.

fmt_cgns.x: A modern `.cgns` is an HDF5 file holding a tree of CGNS nodes, so h5py reads it and the CGNS library is not needed. Unstructured zones, sections of any type or `MIXED`, and `ZoneBC` boundaries (on faces or vertices) are read. Without `ZoneBC`, every surface section becomes a BC with its name.
Tensor hexahedra (HEXA_8/27/64/125) are reordered to the canonical layout. Serendipity ones (HEXA_20…) keep only their corners, and say so.
Not read: CGNS/ADF (the old format, not HDF5: convert it with `adf2hdf`), structured zones and NGON/NFACE polyhedra.

fmt_gmsh.x: Version 2.2 goes through an own parser because **ANSA writes the binary in big-endian**. The format allows it: the integer `1` in the header gives the byte order and gmsh honours it. meshio does not, and fails with a terse "Couldn't read file". `meta['byteorder']` tells you which one it was. Version 4 still goes through meshio.

Physical groups give the names: dimension 3 are zones, dimension 2 are BCs. A physical group declared without elements still shows up, as an empty BC. Surfaces in no physical group are grouped by geometrical entity (`entity_<n>`).

fmt_hmesh.x: The **solution** nodes HORSES3D used, element by element. No connectivity and no BCs: LEGOLAS rebuilds the connectivity by merging coincident nodes. That only works with Gauss-Lobatto nodes, which lie on the faces; with Gauss nodes the elements share nothing, and it warns.
Mind that the order here is the solution order (`p`), not the geometric order of the mesh.

mesh.x: Containers

`Mesh` holds `points` (unique nodes), `blocks` (one `CellBlock` per element kind and order), `boundaries` (one `Boundary` per name), `zones` and `meta`. A cell's global index runs through the blocks in order; `mesh.locate_cell` turns it into (block, local).

A `Boundary` **has no surface cells**: it stores (element, local face) pairs. Face nodes always come from the volume element, so every format ends up with the same face layout, however the file wrote its surfaces.
Canonical node order

head: element
order
layout
rows: tensor, i fastest: node (i, j, k) sits at i + (N+1) j + (N+1)² k. **The linear one too**: its 8 corners are NOT in VTK order (use `ordering.hex_corners`)

mesh.x: It is the order of HOPR and HORSES3D, and with it interpolation and Jacobians are tensor products.
Faces of a hexahedron
This is CGNS's face order and HOPR's `SideInfo` order. `ordering.hex_face_grid(N, face)` returns all the nodes of a face as an outward-oriented (N+1)×(N+1) grid.
Where the permutation tables come from

They were measured, not copied from a manual. gmsh 4.13.1 meshed a unit cube with a single element of order 1 to 4 and wrote it as `.msh` v2.2, `.msh` v4.1 and `.cgns`. Rounding each node's coordinates to the 1/N grid gives its tensor index. Those files live in `FotR/tests/data/legolas/` and the tests repeat the measurement.
The trap they hide: meshio returns `hexahedron27` in VTK order but `hexahedron64` and `hexahedron125` in gmsh's native order. Hence one table for meshio and another for gmsh.

The VTK ones (Lagrange hexahedron and quadrilateral, types 72 and 70) were measured the same way, with VTK 9.5's `GetParametricCoords`, and gmsh's quadrangle on the faces of the same reference cubes. A test checks them against VTK when it is installed.
Order screen

On reading, `io.read` picks 2000 random high-order hexahedra and checks that, along every grid line, nodes always move the same way (`ordering.tensor_monotonic`). A wrong permutation sends some node backwards, and the reader records it in `meta['warnings']`.

nested_Viewer.x: Works without internet: three.js 0.160.0 ships inside the package (`static/three/`, MIT licence), copied untouched from the official npm package, with its sha256 checked by the tests. The page asks for nothing outside its own server.

The server sends surfaces, never the volume: boundaries by name and the cells around the plane. Each request has a budget of **1 million triangles** (about 55 MB with edges); a bigger zone is drawn decimated (1 in k faces) and starts hidden. That happens to `entity_1` in the sphere `.msh`: 1.5 M interior faces, 12 M triangles. Change it with `show(max_triangles=…)`.

`show()` starts a separate process that reads the file again, because reading it is faster than shipping it. A mesh built in memory is saved first to `~/.cache/FotR/legolas/` and the server deletes it once read. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, is read-only and stops after 30 minutes with no page open (the page pings it every minute). For a server inside your own process, `lg.viewer.server().start()`.

Checked on 20/11/2026 in a headless Chromium (QtWebEngine on an Xvnc display, software WebGL) with the turbine g2 and the sphere v1g2: zones, layer, clip, cell picking and views, no console errors. Trying it in your own browser is still yours to do.

nested_Quality.x: Where it is evaluated

For hexahedra of order N, the Jacobian is computed at the (N+1)³ Gauss-Lobatto points from the Lagrange interpolant through the geometric nodes, which every format places **equispaced**; for N = 1 those points are the corners. The volume is the quadrature of det J on them. Linear tetrahedra, prisms and pyramids use the three edges of each corner, normalised so that the regular cell scores 1 (the pyramid apex has four and is skipped).

Orientation: VTK and gmsh number the prism the opposite way round, so in one format every prism may come out "left-handed". Each block keeps the orientation of its majority and only the minority comes out negative; when a whole block was turned round, an `info` says so. TIFON meshes (CODA prisms, gmsh 2.2) always do, and it is not an error.
Checked against what we already knew

Turbine g1, g2 and g4: minimum `jacobian_ratio` 0.46, no negative cells. That is what PyHOPE gave for those meshes (0.4–0.5). The worst cells sit at the corners of the O-grid around the rotor (x = 3.66).

The `my_ESPHERE_1` sphere comes out with `jacobian_ratio` ≈ 0.074 in **every** cell. It is not a bug: the mesh is made of tetrahedra split into four hexahedra, and a hexahedron cut from a regular tetrahedron scores exactly 0.0741, with skewness 1/3 and scaled Jacobian 0.707. That is why the `jacobian_ratio` warning fires at 0.05 and not at 0.1.
In the viewer

**Colour** paints surfaces and cuts by any of these metrics, from blue (better) to red (worse), with the p1–p99 range by default so that a couple of extreme cells do not flatten the scale. Below the legend come the ten worst: a click selects one, moves the cut plane to it if a cut is on, and brings the camera close, looking into the opening. The cell's card adds its metrics.

nested_Resolution.x: Before Helm's Deep Legolas looked across the plain and knew how many were coming and how long they would take. This is the same: look at the mesh before the run and know whether the LES will see what it must. It is mesh design, not post-processing: the real y⁺ comes from the wall shear of a `.hsol`, and that belongs to the HORSES3D tools.

lg.resolution.wall('esphere_surface', p=3)        # 1st cell, 1st node, tangential sizes, growth
lg.resolution.yplus('esphere_surface', Re=400, p=3,
                    correlation='laminar', flow_dir=[1, 0, 0])
print(lg.resolution.report(walls='esphere_surface', p=3, Re=400, correlation='laminar'))
lg.viewer.show(fields=lg.resolution.fields(p=3, walls='esphere_surface', Re=400))

what it is
rows: V^(1/3); and the smallest and largest of the three lengths of a hexahedron (mean of its four edges in each direction, along the curved nodes). For the linear kinds, the shortest and longest edge

nested_Resolution.x: With U = 1 and ν = L/Re, a length y is y·Re·√(Cf/2)/L in wall units. Cf comes from a flat-plate correlation: turbulent 0.026·Re_x^(−1/7) or laminar (Blasius) 0.664·Re_x^(−1/2). Re_x uses each face's distance from the leading edge (the most upstream corner of the zone) when `flow_dir` is given, and L otherwise. It is an estimate to size the first cell, not a prediction of the flow: at a stagnation point or in separated flow it fails by construction.

The report compares with the usual targets of a wall-resolved LES (Piomelli & Chasnov 1996; Georgiadis, Rizzetta & Fureby 2010): y⁺ ≤ 1, Δx⁺ between 50 and 150, Δz⁺ between 15 and 40, and gives the share of faces inside each range.

`my_ESPHERE_1` sphere (v2g2, D = 1, Re = 400, laminar, p = 3): first cell from 0.057 to 0.19 D; first solution node from 0.016 to 0.052 D, with estimated y⁺ from 0.86 to 5.3 (median 1.9). Tangential node spacing ≈ 0.03 D. DG Δ from 0.017 next to the sphere to 0.65 at the outer boundary.

`fields()` returns the per-cell arrays ready for `lg.viewer.show(fields=…)`: size, anisotropy, Δ and, with walls, first cell height and estimated y⁺ of the wall cells (NaN elsewhere). They appear in the **Colour** selector next to the quality metrics, with their legend and their ten worst. The channel takes any per-cell array, not only these.

what it does

Each node is placed in the reference cube by inverting the trilinear map of the corners (which are right: the topology already matched), and the position most voted over 400 cells wins

nested_Convert.x: The case that justifies it (24/11/2026): ANSA's `Wind_turbine_disk_empty_g4.msh`, which PyHOPE rejected ("Connectivity check failed"). `fix_order` finds the permutation with 100 % agreement and leaves 0 cells wrong; `write_msh` rewrites it, gmsh reads it, and **PyHOPE produces an `.h5` identical, dataset by dataset, to the one it produces from the `.cgns`**.

A VTK trap: since 9.1 two edges of the Lagrange hexahedron changed order, and when reading a `.vtu` that declares a version older than 2.2 VTK swaps them back "for compatibility". LEGOLAS writes `version="2.2"`; with another version, ParaView distorts the cells.

head: method
what it does
rows: the honest search: candidate cells by their centroids (k-d tree) and boxes, and Newton on the curved map of each hexahedron (Lagrange through its nodes, any order); in tetrahedra, barycentric coordinates. Returns the cell, ξ in [−1, 1]³, the file's element and, outside, the distance

what HORSES3D's actuator disk really does (`FindActuatorPointElementAD`): each MPI rank takes its **first** element whose *trilinear* shape holds the point, and only there tries the curved one. A point between the chord and the arc of a curved face is lost and the solver stops with "Actuator disk point not found in mesh". Returns which points are found, which would be lost while inside the fluid, and the largest curved |ξ| of each (just above 1 = at risk with another number of ranks)
the stations of an `Act_ActuatorDiskDef.dat` (models A and B), read by position like the solver: plane x = x_hub, angle from +y towards +z

nested_Solution.x: Legolas does not stop at counting orcs: he also watches where they run. `lg.solution` puts a HORSES3D solution on top of the mesh, node by node, and the viewer paints it.

lg.solution.cell_field('u')                   # element mean
lg.solution.load('RESULTS/adA_g2p3_0000500000.hsol', physical=True)   # another, in SI
lg.viewer.show()                              # starts coloured by Mach
How the solution reaches the mesh

A `.hsol` stores, per element, the solution at (p+1)³ Gauss or Gauss-Lobatto nodes, in the element order of the mesh `.h5`. LEGOLAS evaluates each element's polynomial at the geometric nodes of the mesh (equispaced, order Ngeo), and every vertex the viewer draws takes the value of **its own** element: the jumps of a DG solution between elements show as they are, nothing is averaged. Primitive variables (ρ, u, v, w, p, T, Mach, Cp and |V|) are computed at the solution nodes and then interpolated.

Checked against the solver itself (24/11/2026): the LEGOLAS geometry evaluated at the solution nodes reproduces the coordinates of HORSES3D's `.hmesh` to 10⁻¹⁴ (turbine, Gauss nodes, p = 2, 3 and 4; sphere, Gauss-Lobatto, p = 2). Element order, node order and node positions are the solver's.
